text: Next up, the send button that empties state but not the box. Back to our contact form. Now we add a send button. When the form is sent, our code logs the message and empties the state, so the form is ready for the next message. This bit lives in ContactForm.jsx, starting at line ten, with a function called handleSend that takes e. Line eleven calls e.preventDefault so the page doesn't reload. Line twelve logs sent, followed by the message to the console. And line thirteen calls set message with an empty string. The note says it empties the state after sending. Then line fourteen closes the function. Now we want the message box to start empty. So the obvious move, we give it default value with an empty string. Further down the same file from line sixteen is the return. There's a section, a heading that says Contact Us, and on line nineteen, a form whose on submit is handleSend in curly braces. Inside the label message, line twenty-two is the one to watch. A text area tag with default value equals an empty string and onChange set to handleMessageChange. The note marks it wrong. Starting text only, so send cannot empty the box. Line twenty-four is a paragraph showing message.length out of two hundred, and line twenty-five is the send button with type submit. The rest just closes the form, the section, and the component. While the user types, where is my parcel? Everything works, and the count says nineteen out of two hundred. Then the user clicks send. And Figure Twelve shows what we get. The page still says Contact Us, and the message box still reads, where is my parcel? But the count under it says zero out of two hundred. And down in the console, there's one line, sent, where is my parcel? Logged from ContactForm.jsx line twelve. Hmm. The count says the box is empty, but the old message is still in the box. So who is right? Let's replay what happened in order. While the user typed, each key ran handleMessageChange, and message held the text. The user clicked send, and handleSend saved an empty string with set message. React rendered again. Message is now empty, so the count shows zero. But the text area has no value prop, so React writes no text into it on this render. The browser still holds the typed text inside the box, so the box keeps it. So state is right, and the box is out of date. If the user clicks send again, the console proves it. The second log is empty because state holds an empty string. That's Figure Thirteen, the same form after a second click on send with nothing new typed. The box still says, where is my parcel? And the count still says zero out of two hundred. But the console now has two lines. The first, sent, where is my parcel? And the second, just sent with nothing after it.
